John 14:8–9 does not say Jesus is God.

Philip asks Jesus, “Lord, show us the Father,” and Jesus replies, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” In context, Jesus is explaining that he perfectly represents and reveals the Father—not saying that he is literally the same person as the Father.

In fact, the same Gospel repeatedly distinguishes Jesus from God:

Jesus says, “The Father is greater than I.” (John 14:28)

He also says, “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” (John 17:3)

And after his resurrection: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.” (John 20:17)

As for Revelation 1:8, the speaker is identified as “the Lord God… the Almighty”, not explicitly as Jesus. The surrounding passage distinguishes “God” from “Jesus Christ” (Revelation 1:1–2).

Revelation 1:17–18 says, “I am the First and the Last… I was dead, and behold I am alive forevermore.” This is indeed spoken by the risen Jesus in the passage. But saying Jesus has a divine title or attribute is not the same as Jesus explicitly saying, “I am God.” That is the theological conclusion that Christians draw from the text.

So again, let’s distinguish between what Jesus explicitly says and what later theology concludes from certain titles and passages.

Jesus explicitly calls the Father “the only true God” (John 17:3) and calls the Father “my God” (John 20:17). Those statements deserve to be considered alongside the passages being presented as proof of Jesus’ divinity.

2030: The End of the Company
By 2030, one of the most fundamental assumptions of modern society may begin to disappear: the idea that people must belong to a company in order to work.
AI agents, robotics, automation, cloud computing, and blockchain are transforming far more than productivity. They are challenging the very structure of the modern organization—a system in which people gather inside permanent institutions, managers supervise employees, and companies coordinate human labor.

A new model is beginning to emerge.

Instead of massive, permanent organizations, humans and artificial intelligence may form temporary, purpose-driven networks. Organizations may appear when a mission requires them, operate autonomously with AI, and disappear once their purpose has been fulfilled.

The company is not an eternal institution.

Just as money, governments, and industries have evolved throughout history, the concept of the company may now be approaching its next great transformation.

This book explores not only the future of jobs, but something far more fundamental:

What happens when the organization itself begins to disappear?

2030 may not be the year every company vanishes. But it could become the moment when humanity realizes that society may no longer require the traditional company to function.

What will humans do when they no longer need to belong to an organization to create value?

And what kind of civilization will emerge after the company?

This is not simply a book about the future of work.

It is a book about the future of human organization itself.

US vs Indian Solar: What’s the real issue?

The US is challenging India’s solar subsidies and has proposed duties of 125.87% + 123.04% on Indian solar imports. Final decision is still pending.

India exported around 4.5 GW of solar modules in FY26, with the US taking the majority of those exports.

Simple example: if an Indian company sells a solar panel in the US for  Ra 100, these duties can make that panel far more expensive there. Buyers may simply look for panels from other countries.

That means Indian manufacturers could have more panels looking for buyers in India. More supply, tougher competition and lower selling prices can hurt profit margins.

Stocks to watch, from higher to lower export exposure:

🔴 Waaree Energies: ~21% overseas revenue
🟠 Vikram Solar: ~16% exports
🟡 Saatvik Green Energy: limited export exposure
🟡 Solex Energy: limited export exposure
🟢 Premier Energies: ~0.8% exports
🟢 Emmvee: primarily domestic

The interesting part is that not all of them are equally exposed to the US. Some have already shifted towards the domestic market, while Waaree has been building manufacturing capacity in the US.

So don’t just see “US tariff = all solar stocks down.”

The real question is: Who actually sells to the US, who manufactures there, and who will be left fighting for the Indian market?

Park Medi World Limited, which runs the Park Group of Hospitals, has just set up a brand new company that it owns completely. This new company is called Park Medicity Prayagraj Limited, and it officially came into existence on September 8, 2026.

The reason they created this new entity is to build and run a large hospital in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. This will be a 550 bed multi super speciality hospital, meaning it will offer many different medical specialities under one roof.

Interestingly, this hospital project has come through a public private partnership, which means the local municipal corporation in Prayagraj has awarded this project to Park Medi World to build and operate the hospital, rather than the government building it entirely on its own.

Since Park Medi World owns one hundred percent of this new company, there is no conflict of interest here. No related parties or group companies have any special stake in this deal, and everything has been done at arm's length, meaning fairly and without favoritism.

The amount of money involved to start this new subsidiary is quite small at this stage, only about fifteen lakh rupees, used to buy one lakh fifty thousand shares in the new company. This is essentially just the initial seed capital needed to officially register the new entity. 

The bigger investment for actually building the hospital would likely come later.

This move signals that Park Medi World is expanding its footprint beyond its existing markets into a new and significant city. 

Prayagraj is a major religious and administrative hub in Uttar Pradesh, known for large events like the Kumbh Mela which draw enormous crowds, so a large modern hospital there could serve a very large population base that may currently lack access to advanced medical care.

Winning a public private partnership project is also meaningful because governments usually award such contracts only to companies they consider financially capable and credible, so it can be seen as a vote of confidence in Park Medi World's ability to execute large scale healthcare projects. 

Successfully completing this one could also make it easier for the company to win similar hospital contracts in other cities in the future, creating a template for growth through government partnerships rather than only through fully self funded new hospitals.

From a business perspective, once operational, a 550 bed hospital adds a large amount of new bed capacity to the company's overall network, which over the years should translate into a meaningful boost to revenue and profits as the hospital ramps up patient volumes. It also allows Park Medi World to diversify geographically, reducing its dependence on its current cities and giving it a foothold in a fast growing part of Uttar Pradesh.

However, since actual construction, government approvals, staffing, and eventually filling up hospital beds with patients typically take several years, the real financial benefit from this move will likely show up gradually over the coming years rather than immediately. 

In short, this is a long term growth seed being planted today, positioning the company for expanded scale and geographic reach in the healthcare sector over the next several years.

Macro · Producer Inflation

PPI (Producer Price Index) measures how prices received by domestic producers change over time.

Unlike CPI, which focuses on consumer prices, PPI looks further upstream — at inflation pressures faced by businesses and producers.

Why does PPI matter?
• It tracks producer-side inflation
• It can signal future consumer price pressure
• It influences Fed rate expectations
• It can move bonds, the dollar, stocks, gold, and crypto

3 keywords to know PPI:
 Producers · Inflation · Fed

What should traders watch?
→ Headline PPI
→ Core PPI
→ Month-over-month change
→ Services and goods inflation

A hotter-than-expected PPI can suggest that cost pressures are building upstream.

A cooler reading can indicate that inflation pressure is easing before it reaches consumers.
But PPI is not a perfect predictor of CPI.

What matters is whether producer costs are becoming persistent enough to affect margins, pricing, and ultimately the broader inflation trend.
